info.name: otel-shop
info.description:
Drive the otel-shop API through the gateway on http://localhost:3000.

Everything goes through the gateway, because it is the only application service that publishes a port. The other four talk to each other on the compose network.

## How to use this

Run the folders in order, top to bottom. Each one leaves the system in the state the next one expects.

1. **Health** confirms the gateway is up.
2. **Auth** creates an account and logs in. Login sets an httpOnly `access_token` cookie, and Postman's cookie jar holds on to it for every request after that, so there is no token to copy anywhere.
3. **Products** browses the catalogue and stores a real product id in a collection variable.
4. **Cart** adds, reads, updates and removes items.
5. **Checkout** starts a payment and watches it settle.
6. **Errors worth seeing** triggers the failures that are interesting to look at in traces.

Log out sits at the bottom of the Auth folder. Leave it until you are finished, because everything else needs the session it ends.

## Things worth knowing

- Auth is cookie based, not `Authorization: Bearer`. Do not disable the cookie jar.
- Checkout is asynchronous. It answers `202 Accepted` with the payment still `pending`, and the fake provider calls back about 1.5 seconds later. Give it a moment before you read the payment back.
- The catalogue is seeded with 300 products, and every product whose id is 1, 11, 21 and so on is out of stock. That is deliberate, and the Errors folder uses it.
- The gateway rate limits to 20 requests per minute per IP. Clicking through this collection by hand will not hit that, but a loop will.

item.name: 0. Health
item.description: One request to confirm the stack is actually up before you blame anything else.

request.description: The gateway answers this one itself, before the rate limiter and before any proxying. If this fails, nothing else in the collection will work, so check `docker compose ps` first.

item.name: 1. Auth
item.description:
Sign up once, then log in. The gateway proxies all of these straight through to the auth service.

Log out is here too, because it belongs with the rest of auth, but leave it alone until you are finished. It kills your session, and every folder after this one needs it.

request.description:
Creates the account. It does not log you in, so follow it with Log in.

The password rules are strict: at least 8 characters, with a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter and a special character. The phone has to be a valid international number.

Sending this a second time returns a conflict, which is expected. The test below accepts that, so you can re-run the folder without editing anything. If you want a clean account, change the `email` collection variable.

exec: console.log("account already existed, carry on to Log in");

request.description:
The response body is only `{ "message": "success" }`. The useful part is the `Set-Cookie` header, which carries an httpOnly `access_token`.

Postman stores that in its cookie jar against `localhost` and attaches it to the rest of the collection for you. Nothing to copy, nothing to paste.

If later requests come back `401`, open the Cookies link under the Send button and check the cookie is still there and has not expired.

exec: pm.test("an access_token cookie came back", function () {

request.description:
Send this when you are done, not now. Everything below this folder needs the session it ends.

It clears the cookie and blacklists the token's id in Redis, so the token is dead even though it has not expired yet.

That blacklist check is why every authenticated request through the gateway touches Redis, which is a detail worth remembering when you start looking at where your latency goes.

It also answers `200` when you are already logged out, so there is no way to get an error out of it.

item.name: 2. Products
item.description: The catalogue is public, so these work whether or not you logged in. Paging is cursor based on the product id.

request.description:
Returns 20 products at a time, as `{ hasNextPage, products, cursor }`.

The test script picks the first product with stock on hand and saves its id to the `productId` collection variable, so the Cart folder works against something real rather than a hardcoded guess.

exec: pm.test("returns a page of products", function () {

request.description:
Pass the `cursor` from the previous page to get the next one. List products saved it for you.

Keep sending this to walk the catalogue. `hasNextPage` goes false on the last page, and `cursor` is then absent.

Reads a single product.

This one is worth sending twice. The first call misses the cache and hits Postgres, the second is served from Redis, and once the services are instrumented the two traces look visibly different.

item.name: 3. Cart
item.description:
Every cart route needs the login cookie. The cart lives in Redis only, keyed by user, and it calls the products service to resolve each item's name and price as you add it.

Note that adding to the cart does not check stock. That happens at checkout.

Run this folder top to bottom. The last request puts an item back so the Checkout folder has something to pay for.

request.description:
Adds a product to your cart. Sending it again for the same product adds to the existing line rather than creating a second one.

A single line caps at 100 units and a cart caps at 50 distinct products.
Returns the lines in your cart, each with the name, price and currency that were resolved from the products service when you added it.

exec: pm.test("cart has at least one line", function () {

request.description: Sets the line to an absolute quantity, it does not add to it. The product has to already be in the cart, otherwise you get a `404`.
Drops one line. Removing the last line clears the whole cart key out of Redis.
Empties the cart. This is also what the cart service does to itself when it consumes a `payment.succeeded` event from Kafka, which is the step you can watch at the end of the Checkout folder.
You just emptied the cart, and checkout on an empty cart returns a `404`. This puts an item back so the next folder has something to pay for.

exec: pm.test("cart is ready for checkout", function () {

item.name: 4. Checkout
item.description:
This is the interesting one, and the request the article keeps coming back to.

One call fans out across four services and a message broker: payment reads your cart, re-prices it against the products service, reserves the stock, writes a pending payment row, and calls the fake provider. The provider answers immediately and then calls payment back on a webhook about 1.5 seconds later. Payment publishes the outcome to Kafka, where products either marks the stock sold or releases it, and cart empties itself on success.

So the `202` you get back is not the end of the story. Wait a moment, then read the payment back.

request.description:
No body. The cart is the input, and the `x-idempotency-key` header is required.

The pre-request script generates a fresh key every time you send this, so each send starts a new payment. The next request shows what happens when the key repeats.

You get `202 Accepted` with the payment still `pending`. Roughly 80% of payments succeed, which is tunable with `SUCCESS_RATE`, so expect a failure every few runs. That is intentional, since a system that never fails is no use for learning to debug one.

exec: ". give the provider a second or two, then read it back."

item.name: Start a checkout with the same key

request.description:
Same key as the request before it, because this one does not generate a new one.

You get the same payment id back rather than a second charge. Worth sending so you can see how short the trace is compared to the first checkout: it returns on the idempotency lookup and never touches the cart, the products service or the provider.

Your payments, newest first, 20 at a time, paged on a `cursor` that is a payment id.

Send this a couple of seconds after a checkout and the payment you just started should have moved off `pending` to `succeeded` or `failed`. If it is still pending, the provider callback has not landed yet. Send it again.

If it stays pending, something is wrong with the webhook rather than with the payment, and `docker compose logs payment payment-provider` is the place to look.

exec: console.log("payment " + id + " is not on this page");
console.log("still pending, the provider has not called back yet. send this again.");

request.description:
If the payment succeeded, this is empty, and nothing in the request chain you sent emptied it. The cart service did that to itself after consuming `payment.succeeded` from Kafka.

That gap is the point. The HTTP response you got back from checkout tells you nothing about whether this part ever happened, which is exactly the kind of thing you need tracing for.

If the payment failed, the cart is still full, and the stock that was reserved has been released.

item.name: 5. Errors worth seeing
item.description:
Deliberate failures. Each one shows up differently once the services are instrumented, and they are the fastest way to get something red on a dashboard without waiting for a real problem.

The out of stock sequence at the end leaves your cart dirty, so it finishes by clearing it.

request.description:
A `401` from the gateway, which rejects this before it ever reaches the cart service.

Note the host: `127.0.0.1` rather than `localhost`. That is not a typo. Postman keys its cookie jar by domain, and your login cookie was stored against `localhost`, so addressing the same gateway by IP is the simplest way to send an unauthenticated request without clearing cookies and having to log in again.

Every field here is wrong, so the response lists a detail per field. Validation failures like this are worth separating from real faults when you start looking at error rates, because a `400` means the caller was wrong and a `500` means you were.

exec: pm.test("rejected as a bad request", function () {

request.description: A `404` that travels the whole way to Postgres before anyone can say so. The id is valid, it just is not there, so the products service has to miss the cache and then miss the database.
A cart line caps at 100 units, so this is rejected by validation before the cart service calls anything else. Your cart is untouched.

exec: pm.test("rejected as a bad request", function () {

item.name: Add an out of stock product

request.description:
This succeeds, which is the surprising part. The cart does not check stock, it only resolves the product so it can store a name and a price.

The seed data puts every tenth product out of stock, starting at id 1, so ids 1, 11, 21 and so on all have zero quantity.

The failure comes one request later.

exec: pm.test("added, despite having no stock", function () {

request.description:
A `422`, raised by the products service when payment tries to reserve the stock.

This is the most useful failure in the collection. The error surfaces at the gateway, but it was raised two services away, and no payment row and no provider call ever happened. Reading that off the logs alone is miserable. Reading it off one trace is obvious.
Empties the cart so the out of stock item does not block the next checkout you try.
